strengths: Novel and important problem framing: The distinction between explicit ToM (inferring mental states) and applied ToM (using that knowledge) is under-explored and critical for real-world LLM deployment

High-quality dataset: Rigorous crowdworker qualification (19% pass rate), unanimous annotator agreement requirement, diverse scenarios beyond Sally-Anne task paradigm, and implicit mental states requiring genuine commonsense reasoning
Comprehensive and convincing evaluation: Clear performance gap across 10 frontier models (95%+ on mental state vs. 10-59% on applied ToM), robust to prompt variations, thorough intervention analysis
Well-designed experiments: Systematic ablations and scenario-specific analysis effectively demonstrate that poor applied ToM performance is fundamental rather than question-wording artifact
Reproducibility: Dataset and evaluation data publicly released with detailed documentation of all prompts, crowdsourcing procedures, and experimental setup
Clear practical relevance: Findings directly inform safe deployment of LLMs in human-centered environments and highlight risks of relying on models for autonomous reasoning about others' behavior
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: Dataset creation closely follows prior work (Tian et al. 2024), evaluation uses standard accuracy metrics, and all proposed interventions are existing prompt-engineering techniques rather than novel methods

Insufficient root cause analysis: While the gap is clearly demonstrated, the paper provides limited insight into why it occurs—is this a training objective problem, architectural limitation, or reasoning bottleneck? No investigation of whether this is addressable through training

No proposed solutions: All interventions are inference-time workarounds explicitly acknowledged as 'fragile band-aids.' Paper identifies a critical deployment problem but offers no actionable solutions for practitioners

Missing human baseline: No human performance provided, making it unclear whether below-random model performance reflects genuine limitations or difficult questions. Limits strength of claims about model deficiencies

Confounded o1 model evaluation: o1 models use fundamentally different reasoning mechanisms (hidden reasoning tokens), making performance comparison unfair and confounding the analysis of what contributes to applied ToM improvements

Judgment question validity concerns: 'Reasonableness' is inherently subjective. While prompt variants are tested (Appendix F), fundamental ambiguity remains. No inter-annotator agreement metrics reported for judgment questions

Limited error analysis: No systematic categorization of failure types, which behavior predictions fail most frequently, or what properties of scenarios affect difficulty. Post-hoc observations about 'provider info healthcare' but no systematic analysis

Dataset scope limitations: Binary multiple-choice only, 2-sentence stories (may not represent real-world complexity), no nested mental states, English-only, and somewhat artificial scenarios reduce generalizability
Incomplete analysis of why findings matter: While practical relevance is mentioned, specific use cases where this gap is problematic and concrete deployment implications could be much clearer
Presentation: Paper is lengthy (34 pages); key findings on inference costs relegated to appendix; important analysis (inter-annotator agreement) missing; some figures difficult to read

strengths: Rigorous dataset construction with exceptional quality control (19% qualification pass rate, unanimous annotator agreement)
Comprehensive evaluation across 10 frontier models with systematic scenario analysis and clear experimental setup
Addresses limitations of prior ToM datasets by covering diverse real-world information asymmetry scenarios beyond Sally-Anne tasks
Clear conceptual distinction between explicit ToM (mental state inference) and applied ToM (behavior prediction and judgment)
Excellent presentation quality with detailed visualizations and extensive methodological transparency (appendices, reproducibility commitments)
Intentional use of implicit mental states without explicit mentalizing words encourages genuine commonsense reasoning
weaknesses: Limited novelty: The core finding that models fail at downstream application despite excelling at recognition is well-documented in other domains and not inherently surprising
Lack of theoretical insight: Paper is primarily descriptive, showing failures without explaining underlying causes or proposing solutions
Paradoxical intervention results: Simple prompting (MS reminder + CoT*) improves Claude-3.5-Sonnet from 63.3% to 97.1% average accuracy, undermining claims about fundamental ToM limitations

Homogeneous scenario design: All 10 scenarios involve unawareness of negative information; lacks scenarios with positive/neutral information or other ToM types (second-order reasoning, conflicting beliefs)
High story rejection rate (68% filtered out) suggests the implicit false-belief generation process was poorly calibrated and remaining stories may have subtle issues
Insufficient statistical rigor: No error bars, confidence intervals, significance tests, or inter-annotator agreement metrics (only unanimous agreement required)

Judgment question design concerns: Binary questions with 50% random baseline, many models scoring below random, potential confounds with LLM safety training (models may suppress harmful counterfactuals)
Missing human baselines: No human performance data, unclear what constitutes reasonable performance on subjective judgment tasks
Incomplete related work comparison: No direct empirical comparisons to existing ToM datasets; unclear if findings generalize beyond SimpleToM's specific design
No mechanistic analysis: Lacks investigation of model representations, reasoning patterns, or attention mechanisms that might explain the explicit-applied gap

strengths: Addresses important gap in ToM evaluation by distinguishing explicit ToM (mental state inference) from applied ToM (behavior prediction and judgment), filling a real need in the literature
Rigorous dataset creation with strict quality control (19% pass rate on qualification test, 32% retention after filtering, unanimous annotator agreement required)
Comprehensive evaluation of 10 frontier LLMs revealing consistent and substantial performance gaps (e.g., 95.6% to 49.5% to 15.3% across question types for GPT-4o)
Diverse scenarios (10 types) covering different information asymmetries beyond classical false-belief tasks, with implicit rather than explicit mental state cues
Systematic exploration of inference-time interventions with clear documentation and demonstration that near-perfect performance is achievable with appropriate guidance
High-quality presentation with clear figures, detailed documentation, and commitment to dataset release enabling community reproduction and future research
Interesting finding that o1-preview achieves substantially better applied ToM performance, suggesting reasoning-time compute is important
weaknesses: Limited novelty in individual components—dataset creation pipeline (LLM generation + human annotation) and interventions (CoT, system prompts, reminders) are well-established techniques

Conflation of distinct reasoning processes under 'applied ToM' label—behavior prediction may rely more on commonsense goal inference while judgment requires conditional reasonableness evaluation; these should be analyzed separately
Limited theoretical insight into mechanisms causing the explicit/applied ToM gap—documents the phenomenon but provides minimal analysis of why it occurs or what type of reasoning fails
Incomplete failure mode analysis—while some examples provided, systematic categorization of failure types and patterns would strengthen understanding of model limitations

Design choices for applied ToM questions not fully justified—binary judgment of 'correct' actions on 2-sentence stories is somewhat artificial; severity dimension (mild/high) introduced during generation isn't leveraged in analysis
No direct comparison to existing ToM datasets (ToMi, ToM-bAbI, Hi-ToM, BigToM), limiting ability to assess relative difficulty and generalizability of findings
Limited scope—all scenarios involve hidden information/information asymmetry; unclear if gaps generalize to other ToM reasoning patterns (inference, communication, deduction)
Intervention study limitations—interventions are task-specific and ad-hoc rather than principled; no exploration of training-based approaches or fundamental architectural solutions
Missing ablations—no analysis of how filtering strictness affects findings, limited sensitivity analysis for decoding parameters, inter-annotator agreement rates before filtering not reported
Practical guidance for closing the gap is limited; while paper appropriately cautions against deployment, actionable insights for practitioners and researchers are underdeveloped

strengths: Important conceptual distinction between explicit and applied ToM, theoretically motivated by psychology literature and filling a gap in prior work
High-quality dataset with rigorous quality control: 1147 stories, 10 diverse everyday scenarios, implicit mental state cues, 67-71% rejection rate, 19% crowdworker qualification rate
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: 21 models, 10 scenarios, statistical rigor with confidence intervals and bootstrap tests, multiple test-time interventions
Clear and striking empirical finding: ~30-50% performance gap between explicit ToM (~95%) and applied ToM (~50-70% behavior, ~10-40% judgment) consistent across models
Excellent reproducibility: dataset/code release promised, extensive appendices with all prompts and documentation, thoughtful FAQs
Human baseline shows consistency across question types that models lack, validating benchmark design
Well-motivated practical applications (AI assistants, judges, healthcare) with real safety implications
weaknesses: Limited root cause analysis: paper documents the gap but doesn't deeply investigate why it exists; missing error analysis or mechanistic understanding of failure modes

LLM-in-the-loop dataset generation creates potential bias: stories generated by LLMs then filtered by humans; heavy filtering (67-71%) may create non-representative sample; possible circularity with model patterns; no ablation comparing human-written vs. LLM-generated stories
Scope limited to information awareness binary false-belief scenarios; doesn't test desires, emotions, beliefs-about-beliefs, or other mental state aspects

Test-time interventions analysis (Section 5.3) largely confirms expected results without constructive insights; only MS Remind + specific CoT* closes gap, but highly task-specific and doesn't generalize
Human baseline is weak: only 50 stories (5 per scenario); no inter-annotator agreement statistics; cannot confidently claim humans are consistent vs. lucky

Missing ablations and confound analysis: no comparison of model action priors, no analysis of asymmetry in judgment questions (asking about correct actions only), severity levels generated but not analyzed
Shallow mechanistic understanding: gap may simply reflect downstream tasks being harder; doesn't distinguish between reasoning failure vs. compositional failure vs. attention failure
Binary choice format limits nuance; findings about CoT helping somewhat align with prior work rather than being novel

strengths: Well-designed benchmark with diverse scenarios, implicit mentalizing requirements, and rigorous annotation (29-33% retention rate)
Important empirical finding: frontier LLMs excel at explicit ToM (~95%) but struggle with applied ToM (behavior ~50-67%, judgment <25%)
Comprehensive evaluation across 21 models with proper statistical reporting (95% CIs, bootstrap tests)
Clear practical implications for LLM deployment in social applications
High reproducibility with dataset/code release and detailed documentation of methods
weaknesses: Limited novelty: explicit/applied ToM distinction is established in psychology; documenting gap in LLMs is incremental rather than groundbreaking

Gap appears partially artifactual: interventions (MS remind + CoT*) boost judgment from 24.9% to 96.5% for Claude, suggesting capability exists but isn't robustly accessible—more a prompting/brittleness issue than fundamental limitation
Narrow scope: only tests information awareness and false beliefs; ignores desires, emotions, intentions; binary-choice questions simplify real ToM reasoning
Insufficient mechanistic analysis: documents the gap but provides limited investigation of why models struggle or what architectural/training changes would help
Missing key comparisons: no direct evaluation on other ToM benchmarks (ToMi, ToMBench, Hi-ToM, OpenToM) to assess generalization; claims may be benchmark-specific
Human baseline limited to 50 stories (4.4% of dataset); only 5 per scenario type weakens validation of task design
Judgment question concerns: asking 'was that reasonable?' is inherently subjective; <10% accuracy could reflect lack of normative reasoning rather than ToM
Practical utility of proposed interventions is limited: require expensive 200+ token outputs vs. 2-token baseline; improvements in Table 3 often modest

strengths: Clear identification of important gap between explicit ToM (mental state inference) and applied ToM (behavior prediction and judgment), with consistent findings across 21 models
High-quality dataset construction with rigorous quality control: 67-71% filtering rate, high-standard crowdworkers (≥98% approval, Masters level), strict 19% qualification pass rate

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across diverse models (small open-weights to frontier reasoning models like o1-preview and DeepSeek-R1) with proper statistical reporting (95% CIs, bootstrap tests)

Well-motivated design choices grounded in psychology literature, including use of implicit mentalizing language and diverse everyday scenarios (10 information asymmetry types) rather than templated Sally-Anne variants
Diverse scenarios with natural information asymmetries move beyond classical false-belief tasks, testing ToM in realistic contexts like grocery stores, offices, and healthcare
Robust findings across multiple validations: consistent 30%+ performance drop holds across all models, intervention types, and scenario-level analyses; human baseline shows much better consistency

Thorough analysis of test-time interventions revealing that heavy guidance (MS reminder + task-specific CoT) can achieve ~95% but requires question-specific hints, illuminating the fragility of applied ToM
Strong practical relevance with concrete examples of deployment risks in AI assistants and AI judges; clear motivation for why applied ToM matters
Commitment to reproducibility: detailed appendices with all prompts, crowdsourcing instructions, qualification procedures; promises to release dataset and code
weaknesses: Limited scope of ToM aspects tested: only information awareness examined, not other mental states (desires, emotions, goals, intentions) or higher-order beliefs; no complex multi-character scenarios

Judgment task conceptual ambiguity: unclear whether 'reasonableness' tests ethics, social norms, outcomes, or logical consistency; fact that MS reminder + CoT achieves 95% suggests issue may be attention/salience rather than fundamental reasoning

Dataset generated by LLMs then evaluated on same models: potential sampling bias, 67-71% filtering rate could systematically affect what remains, and all generator models are similar top-tier proprietary systems
Human baseline limited to 50/1147 stories (~4%) with selection method and annotation procedure incompletely specified; single annotation per question limits inter-rater agreement assessment

Incomplete failure mode analysis: paper identifies that models fail but not deeply why—whether confusing percepts, failing tracking through reasoning chains, or applying wrong heuristics; Appendices M and N provide limited systematic error analysis

Interventions analyzed are basic (reminders, system prompts, generic/CoT) with no exploration of architectural changes, training approaches, or whether fundamental capability exists but isn't activated
Limited analysis of scenario variation: healthcare provider scenario gets much higher behavior prediction scores (possibly due to safety training), but causes not thoroughly investigated
Related work positioning somewhat brief relative to crowded recent ToM benchmark landscape (ToMBench, OpenToM, Hi-ToM, BigToM); could better clarify unique contributions vs. concurrent work
Key statistical details (bootstrap CIs, one-sided p-values) relegated to Appendix Q rather than main text; Table 3 interventions shown only for 3 models rather than all 21

Questions about generalizability: unclear how findings vary across model families, whether results depend on training data containing similar scenarios, or how they would extend to more complex social reasoning
